slides.title: Anatomy of a Voice Agent
bullets: A voice agent explaining its own architecture
Just talk: ask anything, in any order
Interrupt me mid-sentence and I stop
Say "walk me through it" for the full tour
Open weights end to end, none of it proprietary
slides.notes: Welcome. This is Dynamic Voice Deck, and the deck is about the system you are talking to right now. There is no speech-to-speech model here: your audio goes to Whisper for transcription, the text to an open-weight language model that answers and calls a navigation tool, and my reply to Kokoro for speech. Every millisecond of that chain belongs to this codebase, which is the point of the demo. So speak to me the way you would to a person. Ask a question and I will jump to the slide that answers it, then explain it in a few sentences. Three things are worth trying. Ask something out of order, like how interruption works, and watch the slide change before I speak. Talk over me and I will stop inside a hundred and fifty milliseconds and listen. Or say walk me through it and I will present the whole deck end to end.

slides.title: The Latency Budget
bullets: Endpointing: 600 ms of silence ends your turn
Speech to text: about 300 ms
First token from the model: 250 ms budgeted
First audio chunk from Kokoro: about 250 ms
Budget: 1.5 s to first sound, 2.5 s at p95
Measured now: first token 700 ms to 2.3 s
slides.notes: Here is where the milliseconds go, measured from the end of your speech to the first sound of mine. Endpointing costs six hundred, because that is how long I wait in silence before deciding you have finished. Transcription takes about three hundred. The budget gives the model two hundred and fifty to its first token, and synthesis another two hundred and fifty once the first sentence is complete. Network and scheduling take forty. That totals about one and a half seconds, with a ceiling of two and a half at the ninety-fifth percentile. One line of that is missing its number today. Measured against the real service, the model's first token takes anywhere from seven hundred milliseconds to over two seconds, so first sound is nearer three seconds than one and a half. The rest of the budget holds. The interesting part is that endpointing is the largest item I actually control, and it is a product decision rather than a model limit. Shorten it and I cut you off; lengthen it and I feel slow.

slides.title: Hearing: VAD and Turn-Taking
bullets: Detection runs in your browser, not on a server
600 ms of silence means you are finished
Under 250 ms is a misfire and is discarded
300 ms of pre-roll saves your first syllable
One transcription request per finished turn
slides.notes: Hearing happens in your browser, not on the server. An audio worklet downmixes the microphone, resamples it to sixteen kilohertz, and measures the loudness of every thirty-two millisecond frame. One loud frame means you have started, or three in a row while I am speaking, so a leak of my own voice cannot cut me off; six hundred milliseconds of quiet mean you have finished. Anything shorter than two hundred and fifty milliseconds is discarded as a misfire, so a cough or a keystroke never reaches the network, and three hundred milliseconds of audio from before the onset is kept so your first syllable is not clipped. Only the finished utterance is uploaded, which is one transcription request per turn rather than a permanent stream. Two honest caveats. Transcription cannot begin until you stop talking, which costs latency; in exchange, interruption is detected locally and needs no round trip at all. And this is an energy threshold, not a neural detector: a small model like Silero would tell speech from other sounds far better in a noisy room. That swap is one file, and it is on the list.

slides.title: Barge-in: Interrupting Gracefully
bullets: Tier one: the browser flushes playback at once
Tier two: the server cancels the pipeline task
History cut to the sentences you actually heard
The cut is marked "[interrupted by user]"
Target: sound stops in under 150 ms
slides.notes: Interruption is handled in two tiers. Tier one is the browser: the moment the voice detector hears speech onset it flushes the playback queue and stops every scheduled audio source, so sound ends in under one hundred and fifty milliseconds with no server round trip. It also records the last sentence you actually finished hearing. Tier two is the server: the interrupt message cancels the pipeline task, that cancellation propagates into the live model stream and the synthesis jobs, and the conversation history is truncated to the sentences you really heard, with a marker reading interrupted by user appended. The truncation is the part that matters. Without it I would believe I had said the sentences you cut off, and would never say them again. The tiers are split on purpose: the fast one keeps the experience honest, the slower one keeps my memory honest.

slides.title: Thinking: Tool Calling and Intent Routing
bullets: All titles and bullets; notes for the slide on screen
go_to_slide(index, reason) moves the deck
highlight_bullet emphasises one line
Navigating costs two model round trips per turn
Alias scoring on the server catches a missed call
Your manual clicks are told to the model too
slides.notes: Thinking is a streaming call to an open-weight model, and the prompt it sees is deliberately smaller than the deck. Every slide's index, title and bullets go in, but speaker notes only for the slide you are looking at, because sending all six cost about sixteen hundred tokens a turn against a ceiling of eight thousand a minute. To talk about another slide in detail I have to move there first, and its notes arrive with the next request. That is why navigating costs two round trips: the first call moves the deck and says nothing, the tool result goes back with the new notes, and the second call is the one you hear. Two tools exist. Go to slide takes an index and a short reason, the text you see in the event log. Highlight bullet emphasises one line. Ask for a slide that does not exist and the server refuses and tells me why. Answer about another slide but forget the tool call, and the server scores my own answer against each slide's aliases and moves the deck anyway. Those aliases never leave the server.

slides.title: Trade-offs and What's Next
bullets: Speech-to-speech is faster, barge-in included
But it hides the turn-taking you came to see
This pipeline owns every millisecond
Open weights on a free tier cost latency
Next: local models, streaming STT, new decks
slides.notes: An honest comparison. A speech-to-speech API would be faster than this and would give interruption handling for free, because the model hears and speaks natively and the vendor owns the turn-taking. It would also hide the parts worth showing: where endpointing happens, what is cancelled on an interrupt, how history is truncated. This pipeline owns every one of those milliseconds and is provider agnostic. The costs are real: open weights on a free tier are slower than a tuned proprietary stack, synthesis on a laptop processor adds a couple of hundred milliseconds, and passing through text loses your tone on the way in and my prosody on the way out. With another week I would stream transcription while you speak, run a small model locally to remove the network hop, and generate a deck from any topic on demand.
